introduction-the-distributed-python-prob.core: Python runs one thread of bytecode at a time (the GIL), and multiprocessing is limited to one machine. Ray gives Python a simple API for running functions and classes across a cluster, handling scheduling, data transfer and fault tolerance.

first_principles.problem: Hyperparameter search over 1,000 configs runs for days on one machine.
truths: The GIL limits CPU parallelism within a process.
derivation: Pass data through a **shared object store**.

analogy.title: A dispatch office for a delivery fleet
analogy.story: You hand the office jobs; it assigns drivers across the city and tracks completion.
analogy.breaks: Drivers are independent; Ray tasks can depend on each other's outputs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Near-linear speedup with minimal code changes.

points: GIL and one machine limit Python.

check.q: Why doesn't multiprocessing solve cluster-scale work?
check.a: It only uses cores on one machine and doesn't handle cross-machine scheduling or data transfer.

core-concept-tasks-remote-functions.core: Decorating a function with @ray.remote makes .remote() calls run asynchronously on any worker and return an ObjectRef (a future). ray.get() fetches results, and passing ObjectRefs into other tasks builds a dependency graph without moving data through the driver.

first_principles.problem: We want to parallelise a stateless function across a cluster without writing RPC code.
truths: Futures let you launch first and collect later.
Dependencies can be expressed by passing futures.

analogy.title: Dropping off clothes at a laundry
analogy.story: You get a ticket now and pick up the clean clothes later.
analogy.breaks: You can hand a ticket to another shop as input; real laundry tickets don't chain.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 1,000 tasks scheduled across the cluster at once.

code.text:
import ray
ray.init()

@ray.remote
def square(x):
    return x * x

refs = [square.remote(i) for i in range(1000)]
print(sum(ray.get(refs)))

check.q: Why is ray.get inside a loop an anti-pattern?
check.a: It blocks on each task in turn, serialising work that could run in parallel.

core-concept-actors-stateful-services.core: An actor is a remote instance of a class: a dedicated worker process holding state, whose method calls run serially in order. Actors suit things like a model loaded once on a GPU, a parameter server, a counter or a simulator.

first_principles.problem: Reloading a 10 GB model for every inference task wastes minutes.
truths: Loading expensive resources once saves time.

analogy.title: A dedicated specialist at a desk
analogy.story: Instead of briefing a new temp each time, you send all requests to the expert who already knows the case.
analogy.breaks: If the specialist leaves, their knowledge goes too; actor state is lost on crash unless checkpointed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Model loads once; batches stream through.

check.q: When would you use an actor instead of a task?
check.a: When work needs persistent state or an expensive resource like a loaded model kept between calls.

ray-architecture-the-object-store-and-cl.core: A Ray cluster has a head node (Global Control Store for metadata, cluster dashboard) and worker nodes, each running a raylet (local scheduler and resource manager) plus a shared-memory Plasma object store. Large objects are stored once per node and read zero-copy, and are transferred between nodes on demand.

first_principles.problem: Tasks slow to a crawl and nodes run out of memory, and nobody knows why.
truths: Shared memory avoids copies within a node.
Distributed scheduling avoids a central bottleneck.
Object memory is finite and spills to disk.
derivation: **Raylet** per node schedules locally, spills over to others.

analogy.title: Regional warehouses with a central registry
analogy.story: Each region stores goods locally and ships between regions only when needed; the registry knows where everything is.
analogy.breaks: Warehouses keep goods indefinitely; Ray frees objects when no references remain.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One copy per node instead of 100 serialisations.

check.q: Why use ray.put for a large input shared by many tasks?
check.a: It stores the object once in the object store instead of serialising it with every task call.

ray-ecosystem-high-level-libraries.core: On top of tasks and actors, Ray provides libraries: Ray Data (distributed preprocessing and streaming), Ray Train (distributed training wrappers), Ray Tune (hyperparameter search), Ray Serve (model serving) and RLlib (reinforcement learning). The same cluster runs the whole ML lifecycle.

first_principles.problem: Teams glue Spark, Horovod, Optuna and a separate serving stack, each with its own cluster.
truths: One runtime reduces glue and data movement.
derivation: **Ray Tune** for search with early stopping.

analogy.title: A Swiss Army knife built on one handle
analogy.story: Different blades for different jobs, all sharing the same grip.
analogy.breaks: A specialist tool sometimes beats the multi-tool, e.g. Spark for heavy SQL ETL.

code.text:
from ray import tune
tuner = tune.Tuner(train_fn,
    param_space={'lr': tune.loguniform(1e-5, 1e-2)},
    tune_config=tune.TuneConfig(num_samples=200, scheduler=tune.schedulers.ASHAScheduler()))
tuner.fit()
